A loop that tests `i < 10` and then runs `i--` moves away from 10, so the test stays true and the loop never ends. It is almost always a typo: `--` for `++`, or `<` for `>`.

The rule looks at `++`, `--`, `+=` and `-=` on the counter. If it cannot tell whether the step is positive or negative, it reports nothing.

This rule is on by default.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i--) {
  render(items[i]);
}
```

{/* bad */}
```js
for (let i = items.length - 1; i >= 0; i += 1) {
  render(items[i]);
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  render(items[i]);
}

for (let i = items.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
  render(items[i]);
}
```

The sign of `step` is not known here, so the loop is left alone:

{/* good */}
```js
function walk(items, step) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += step) {
    render(items[i]);
  }
}
```
